title: Karna's abandonment
hook: a son is born shining, in armor and earrings, and his young mother sets him on the river

segments.voice: Yesterday, Karna's abandonment began: Pritha, Durvasa's mantra, and the sun answering a girl's curiosity. Did you pause before trying something just to see? Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

A baby is born in secret, and he's already dressed for battle. That's how the Mahabharata describes him: born wearing armor that's part of his own body, with bright earrings in his ears, shining like his father, the sun. Any other newborn would be scandal enough for an unmarried girl in a king's house. This one glows. There's no hiding him in a corner. And his mother is still very young, still living as a daughter under her father's roof. Today is the day the abandonment actually happens.
screen: `BORN IN SECRET.` → `ARMOR AND EARRINGS.` → `SHINING LIKE THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Kunti's choice is quick in the telling, and heavy in the hearing. Afraid of what her family and the world will say, she places her newborn son in a basket and sets it on the river. In one later part of the poem, the scene is told again at length: she weeps over the basket and speaks to the child, asking the gods of the waters, the sky and the earth to keep him safe, and saying that whoever finds him will be blessed to raise him. Then the current carries him away. Listen to the word the text chooses. It doesn't call her cruel. It calls her afraid. It tells us exactly why, and then it lets us watch her grief. Some readers hear a mother failing her child. Some hear a frightened girl doing the only thing she could see to do. Some hear both at once, and the poem seems to allow that. And notice the armor. The baby is sent off alone, but he isn't sent off unprotected. Whatever the river does, he's wrapped in his father's gift. Those earrings and that armor will matter enormously later, in a scene we'll come to. For now they're a quiet promise in the basket. The word abandonment can sound like a verdict. In this story, it's also an event with a person on each side of it. A mother on the bank. A child on the water. And the Mahabharata will spend a very long time following both of them.
screen: `SHE SETS HIM ON THE RIVER.` · `THE TEXT SAYS: AFRAID.` · `A FAILURE, A FEAR, OR BOTH?` · `WRAPPED IN HIS FATHER'S GIFT.` · then, large: `A PERSON ON EACH SIDE.`

segments.voice: This one is tender, so take your time. Let the breath move slowly. Let one decision come to mind that someone made about you before you could have a say: a move, a parting, a name. You don't need to forgive it or defend it. Just see that there was a person on the other side, deciding. Then notice what went with you anyway, the way the armor went with the child: something that kept you. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Karna's abandonment. A son born shining in armor and earrings, set adrift by a frightened mother who blessed him as he went.
Your line: Karna's abandonment. Today, when you hear about someone's hard choice, look for the fear behind it before you judge. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Some retellings of the Mahabharata, in storytelling, dance and theater, linger on Kunti at the riverbank, letting audiences sit with her grief rather than rushing past it.

original.note: Sanskrit kavaca: armor; Karna's is part of his own body from birth.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mother throws away her baby.
what it means: a frightened girl sets her son adrift, weeping and asking the gods to keep him safe.
what a scholar hears: the abandonment is told briefly in the Adi Parva and told again at length later in the poem, with Kunti's lament at the river.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (birth of Kunti's son with armor and earrings; he is set on the water)
Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Kundalaharana Parva (Kunti's lament as she sets the basket on the river)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm that the Adi Parva gives Kunti's fear of her relatives/the world as the reason, and that the Vana Parva (Kundalaharana) retells the scene with her lament invoking the gods of water, sky and earth.
Confirm 'basket' (Ganguli may say basket or box/chest); the river's name is deliberately left out.
The 'some readers' views are the script's framing, given without ranking.
